newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England says interest rates should rise.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England says interest rates should rise.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George would like to see official interest rates raised to 6.0 percent to prevent a resurgence in inflation, according to minutes of a monetary meeting published on Wednesday.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke rejected his advice at their meeting on July 30, leaving interest rates at 5.75 percent, but pledged to tighten policy if prices started to take off again.
The minutes quoted George as saying the latest economic evidence showed a pickup in consumer-led demand.
"On that basis, the Bank saw no justification for further policy stimulus. In fact, as the Chancellor knew, the Bank would prefer short-term rates at 6.0 percent," the minutes said.
George said it was possible that recent data exaggerated the underlying acceleration of demand.
"But the opposite risk was that if the acceleration continued through the summer and into the autumn, it would become increasingly difficult to moderate."
Official figures released on Wednesday showed a stronger than expected acceleration in retail sales in August.
Clarke, who has the final say on monetary policy, has cut rates four times since December, giving millions of home-owners their cheapest mortgages for a generation.
A general election is due within the next eight months and, with the ruling Conservatives well behind the opposition Labour party in opinion polls, Clarke will be reluctant to raise interest rates.
Clarke told the central bank chief that recent statistics confirmed his expectation that inflation was headed lower.
"He was inclined to leave interest rates unchanged. If inflation pressures started to pick up as a result of stronger growth, there would clearly be a case for tightening policy."
"He was prepared to act pre-emptively, as he had done in 1994. But he saw no evidence yet of those pressures," the minutes said.

The chancellor said his expectation of stronger growth in the second half of the year was undiminished, but he made clear he did not regard this as a cause for concern as growth in recent quarters had been slower than expected.
